title: Perception Agents — Antje Barth, Amazon AGI Lab
talk_summary: Antje Barth argues that agents can now act (click, type, call APIs) but fail at end-to-end reliability because most knowledge work isn't verifiable like code; the fix is 'perception agents' that read the rendered screen, watch the results of their own actions, and verify against explicit specs. She demos two open-source harness pieces: a Chrome annotation extension that captures precise on-screen intent, and a verification loop that checks rendered output against a design.md spec plus automated user-flow walkthroughs.

takeaways.what_they_do: Agent checks its own rendered output against an explicit rules file (design.md: colors, components, layout), auto-generating the rules if absent, then writes a pass/fail report.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can describe in a design MD file what your design rules are... the agent can actually check its own work against those design specs

takeaways.what_they_do: Verification agent drives the app like a real user (add task, delete task) to exercise flows, not just static checks, then reports which passed.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it actually walks through this experience through the app... it might add a task, it might delete a task like a real user would

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of long prose prompts, user selects exact on-screen elements; the tool captures location, style, and a structured summary the agent consumes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: This is a much more precise signal and less lossy than text. and the agent can act exactly on what you marked.

takeaways.what_they_do: Agents should observe the outcome of each action and recover, rather than firing actions and moving on.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if they fire off actions, what they usually do, they move on. They don't watch what happens or recover if one step didn't succeed

takeaways.what_they_do: Argues reliability only compounds where answers are verifiable (code), so invest in making tasks checkable rather than adding capability.
takeaways.evidence_quote: It's because code is verifiable. You can run it, you can test it, you can check it
